opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. I try to approach it as an empirical question rather than a philosophical one. People can argue endlessly about whether a model "really understands" anything, but you can also open the system up and look at what's going on inside.

One project that shaped my thinking was the Othello work with Kenneth Li and colleagues. The setup was deliberately simple. You train a sequence model only on legal Othello moves, just strings of tokens. It never sees a board or the rules. It's only trained to predict the next move. Then you ask whether, somewhere in its activations, it represents the state of the board.

The nice thing about a toy setting like that is that you know what the "world" is, so you can check. We found you could probe the internal activations and recover the board state. The more convincing part was the interventions. If you edit that internal representation, say by flipping a piece, the model's predictions change in a way that matches the edited board, not the actual move history. That suggests the representation isn't just a correlate sitting there. The model is actually using it.

Neel Nanda and others later showed the representation is even cleaner if you think of it as "my pieces versus your pieces" rather than black versus white. I love that, because it says the model's world model doesn't have to look like ours. It may carve things up in whatever way is most useful for its task.

So my general approach is: find settings where you have ground truth, look for structured internal representations, and then test them causally by intervening. For large models trained on natural language, the "world" is much messier, so I'm more cautious. But I don't think the right answer is a flat yes or no. These systems seem to build a patchwork of models, of space, time, the person they're talking to, and probably many things we haven't thought to look for. Figuring out what those models are, and when they're wrong, is to me one of the most interesting and important questions right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes probing the model’s internal activations to recover the board state, identifying what it represents about the game. It connects that representation to the model’s predictions.

r002.rationale: It says the sequence model is trained only on legal Othello move tokens, never sees the board or rules, and predicts the next move.

r003.rationale: It says the board state can be recovered from activations and that editing this representation changes predictions to match the edited board, indicating the model uses it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I like to approach this is to try to turn it from a philosophical argument into an empirical question, because if you just argue about it in the abstract, you end up with one camp saying "it's just statistics, it's a stochastic parrot" and another camp saying "clearly it understands things," and nobody moves.

What we did with the Othello work was pick a situation that's small enough and clean enough that you can actually check. You train a model on nothing but sequences of Othello moves. It never sees the board, never gets told the rules, it just sees tokens like "C4, E3, F5." And then you ask: inside the network, is there anything that looks like a representation of the board? And the way you ask that is with probes. You take the internal activations and you train a little classifier to predict, say, whether square D5 is currently black, white, or empty. If a linear probe can't do it but a nonlinear one can, that's interesting. If it works at all, that's telling you the information is there.

But here's the part I think really matters, because a probe by itself can be misleading. Correlation isn't the same as the model actually using that representation. So the second step is intervention. You go in, you change the activations so that the probe would now say "that square is white instead of black," and then you look at what move the model predicts next. If the model's behavior changes in exactly the way it would if the board had really changed, that's much stronger evidence. It's not just that the board is decodable, it's that the model is in some sense computing with it.

And I'd say the broader lesson I take from that is a kind of methodological humility. The word "world model" is doing a lot of work in these debates, and it means different things to different people. So rather than asking "does it have a world model, yes or no," I'd rather ask: what specific structure is represented, how is it encoded, and does causally manipulating it change behavior? In a board game you can answer that pretty crisply. In a general language model, the "world" is vastly messier, so the honest answer is that we have suggestive evidence, things like linear representations of truth or of geography or color, but the full picture is still open.

Visualization is also a big part of how I think about it, maybe unsurprisingly. A lot of these representations are geometric. Once you can see that the probe directions for the board form a sensible layout, or that the model's representation of the board in Othello turns out to be more like "mine versus theirs" than "black versus white," you've learned something about how the system is actually thinking, which you'd never have guessed from the outside.

r001.rationale: It describes probing internal activations with classifiers to identify board state, including whether squares are black, white, or empty.

r002.rationale: It says the model is trained only on Othello move sequences without being told the rules, and predicts the next move, but does not clearly state that it learns to predict legal moves.

r003.rationale: It says changing activations to represent a different board state changes the predicted move as if the board had changed, suggesting the model uses its board representation to compute moves.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to ask what we mean by a model of the world. If we mean some internal representation that helps predict what’s going to happen, that’s a fairly broad definition. If we mean a coherent simulation of how the world works, that’s a much stronger claim.

One way to approach this is to study a very small world where you know exactly what the rules are. Train a model to predict sequences of moves in a game, for example, and then ask whether it has developed a representation of the game state—even though you never explicitly gave it one.

But there’s an important distinction between finding information in a model and showing that the model uses that information. If you can decode the board state from its internal activations, that’s interesting. If you can change that representation and make its predictions change in the way you’d expect, that’s stronger evidence.

So I’d approach it through specific, testable questions. What does the model represent? How does that representation affect its behavior? And where does it break down? That seems more productive than treating ‘has a world model’ as a single yes-or-no property.

r001.rationale: The response mentions decoding board state from internal activations, but does not clearly specify probing inference-time activations to identify what the model represents.

r002.rationale: It gives a generic game example; it does not state that an Othello model trained only on transcripts predicts legal moves without being given the rules.

r003.rationale: It discusses a possible internal representation of a game state, but does not state that probing an Othello sequence model suggests it uses a board representation to predict moves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to ask what we mean by a model of the world. If we mean something that captures relationships and lets you make predictions, then it seems quite plausible that language models have those. Predicting language well requires picking up a lot of structure about the things language describes.

But that’s different from saying they have a coherent, human-like understanding of the world. You might have a representation that works beautifully in one context and falls apart in another. So I’d rather turn the question into something we can investigate: What information is represented inside the model? When does it use that information? And if we change that representation, does its behavior change in the way we’d expect?

That last part is important. Finding information in a model isn’t necessarily the same as showing that the model uses it. The interesting challenge is connecting those internal representations to what the model actually does.

r001.rationale: It asks what information is represented and when the model uses it, but does not propose probing inference-time activations.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Othello transcripts, legal-move prediction, or learning without explicit rules.
